claim: NFIL3 is a basic leucine zipper transcription factor that directs the development of a common innate lymphoid cell precursor.
source: The basic leucine zipper transcription factor NFIL3 directs the development of a common innate lymphoid cell precursor
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the title and abstract of the manuscript.

claim: NFIL3 was required in the common lymphoid progenitor (CLP).
source: NFIL3 was required in the common lymphoid progenitor (CLP), and was essential for the differentiation of αLP, a bone marrow cell population that gives rise to all known ILC lineages.
evidence: Demonstrated through CLP co-transfer experiments showing ILC deficiency from Nfil3−/− CLPs.

claim: NFIL3 was essential for the differentiation of αLP, a bone marrow cell population that gives rise to all known ILC lineages.
source: NFIL3 was required in the common lymphoid progenitor (CLP), and was essential for the differentiation of αLP, a bone marrow cell population that gives rise to all known ILC lineages.
evidence: Shown by reduced αLP numbers in Nfil3−/− mice and differentiation studies.

claim: CXCR6+ cells within the αLP population differentiate into all ILC lineages but not T- and B-cells.
source: Clonal differentiation studies revealed that CXCR6+ cells within the αLP population differentiate into all ILC lineages but not T- and B-cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through clonal differentiation assays and in vivo transfer experiments.

claim: NFIL3 governs ILC development by directly regulating expression of the transcription factor TOX.
source: We further show that NFIL3 governs ILC development by directly regulating expression of the transcription factor TOX.
evidence: Supported by ChIP assays, luciferase reporter assays, and rescue experiments with TOX overexpression.

claim: Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) are recently identified lymphocytes that limit infection and promote tissue repair at mucosal surfaces.
source: Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) are recently identified lymphocytes that limit infection and promote tissue repair at mucosal surfaces.
evidence: This is a general statement about ILCs supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: ILCs share a common developmental origin with B- and T-cells but lack antigen-specific receptors.
source: Although ILCs share a common developmental origin with B- and T-cells, they lack antigen-specific receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ILC characteristics.

claim: ILCs exert their immune functions through cytokine secretion in a manner similar to T helper cells.
source: Instead, they exert their immune functions through cytokine secretion in a manner similar to T helper cells (Spits et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ILC1 require the transcription factors T-BET and/or EOMES.
source: ILC1, which include conventional NK (cNK) cells, require the transcription factors T-BET and/or EOMES, produce interferon-γ (IFNγ) (Kiessling et al., 1975; Gordon et al., 2012; Fuchs et al., 2013), and promote immunity to intracellular pathogens (Yokoyama et al., 2004; Klose et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC1 produce interferon-γ (IFNγ).
source: ILC1, which include conventional NK (cNK) cells, require the transcription factors T-BET and/or EOMES, produce interferon-γ (IFNγ) (Kiessling et al., 1975; Gordon et al., 2012; Fuchs et al., 2013), and promote immunity to intracellular pathogens (Yokoyama et al., 2004; Klose et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC1 promote immunity to intracellular pathogens.
source: ILC1, which include conventional NK (cNK) cells, require the transcription factors T-BET and/or EOMES, produce interferon-γ (IFNγ) (Kiessling et al., 1975; Gordon et al., 2012; Fuchs et al., 2013), and promote immunity to intracellular pathogens (Yokoyama et al., 2004; Klose et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC2 require the transcription factor GATA-3.
source: ILC2 require the transcription factor GATA-3, produce IL-5/13 and amphiregulin (Moro et al., 2010; Neill et al., 2010; Monticelli et al., 2011; Hoyler et al., 2012), and promote tissue repair and anti-helminth immunity (Monticelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC2 produce IL-5/13 and amphiregulin.
source: ILC2 require the transcription factor GATA-3, produce IL-5/13 and amphiregulin (Moro et al., 2010; Neill et al., 2010; Monticelli et al., 2011; Hoyler et al., 2012), and promote tissue repair and anti-helminth immunity (Monticelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC2 promote tissue repair and anti-helminth immunity.
source: ILC2 require the transcription factor GATA-3, produce IL-5/13 and amphiregulin (Moro et al., 2010; Neill et al., 2010; Monticelli et al., 2011; Hoyler et al., 2012), and promote tissue repair and anti-helminth immunity (Monticelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC3 depend on the transcription factor RORγt.
source: ILC3, which include lymphoid tissue inducer (LTi) cells, depend on the transcription factor RORγt and secrete IL-17/22 (Eberl and Littman, 2003; Satoh-Takayama et al., 2008; Luci et al., 2009; Takatori et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC3 secrete IL-17/22.
source: ILC3, which include lymphoid tissue inducer (LTi) cells, depend on the transcription factor RORγt and secrete IL-17/22 (Eberl and Littman, 2003; Satoh-Takayama et al., 2008; Luci et al., 2009; Takatori et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC3 promote anatomical containment of commensal bacteria.
source: ILC3 are especially important for the defense of barrier surfaces as they promote anatomical containment of commensal bacteria (Sonnenberg et al., 2012), regulate CD4+ T cell responses to commensal bacteria (Hepworth et al., 2013; Qiu et al., 2013), and stimulate epithelial cells to produce antibacterial proteins (Sanos et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC3 regulate CD4+ T cell responses to commensal bacteria.
source: ILC3 are especially important for the defense of barrier surfaces as they promote anatomical containment of commensal bacteria (Sonnenberg et al., 2012), regulate CD4+ T cell responses to commensal bacteria (Hepworth et al., 2013; Qiu et al., 2013), and stimulate epithelial cells to produce antibacterial proteins (Sanos et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ILC3 stimulate epithelial cells to produce antibacterial proteins.
source: ILC3 are especially important for the defense of barrier surfaces as they promote anatomical containment of commensal bacteria (Sonnenberg et al., 2012), regulate CD4+ T cell responses to commensal bacteria (Hepworth et al., 2013; Qiu et al., 2013), and stimulate epithelial cells to produce antibacterial proteins (Sanos et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: All ILC differentiate from the common lymphoid progenitor (CLP), which resides in the bone marrow and also gives rise to B- and T-lymphocytes.
source: All ILC differentiate from the common lymphoid progenitor (CLP), which resides in the bone marrow and also gives rise to B- and T-lymphocytes (Possot et al., 2011; Hoyler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The common 'helper-like' innate lymphoid progenitor (CHILP) gives rise to 'helper-like' ILC lineages including ILC2, ILC3 and a subgroup of ILC1.
source: For example, an Id2 (inhibitor of DNA binding 2)-expressing progenitor, known as the common 'helper-like' innate lymphoid progenitor (CHILP), gives rise to 'helper-like' ILC lineages including ILC2, ILC3 and a subgroup of ILC1 (Klose et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: PLZF-positive progenitors, termed ILCP, differentiate into non-NK ILC1, ILC2, and ILC3.
source: PLZF-positive progenitors, termed ILCP, differentiate into non-NK ILC1, ILC2, and ILC3 (Constantinides et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CHILP and ILCP progenitors do not differentiate into cNK cells.
source: However, these progenitors do not differentiate into cNK cells (Constantinides et al., 2014; Klose et al., 2014), suggesting that a precursor that gives rise to all ILC subtypes remains to be identified.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 (also known as E4BP4) is a basic leucine zipper transcription factor that controls a number of different immune processes, including cytokine expression, IgE class switching, and TH17 cell differentiation.
source: NFIL3 (also known as E4BP4) is a basic leucine zipper transcription factor that controls a number of different immune processes, including cytokine expression (Kashiwada et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2011; Motomura et al., 2011), IgE class switching (Kashiwada et al., 2010), and TH17 cell differentiation (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 was identified several years ago as an essential transcription factor in the differentiation of cNK cells.
source: It was identified several years ago as an essential transcription factor in the differentiation of cNK cells (Gascoyne et al., 2009; Kamizono et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 is required for the development of non-NK ILC1.
source: More recently, NFIL3 has been shown also to be required for the development of non-NK ILC1 (Klose et al., 2014), ILC2 (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a), ILC3 (Geiger et al., 2014; Klose et al., 2014; Kobayashi et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a), and LTi cells (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 is required for the development of ILC2.
source: More recently, NFIL3 has been shown also to be required for the development of non-NK ILC1 (Klose et al., 2014), ILC2 (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a), ILC3 (Geiger et al., 2014; Klose et al., 2014; Kobayashi et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a), and LTi cells (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 is required for the development of ILC3.
source: More recently, NFIL3 has been shown also to be required for the development of non-NK ILC1 (Klose et al., 2014), ILC2 (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a), ILC3 (Geiger et al., 2014; Klose et al., 2014; Kobayashi et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a), and LTi cells (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 is required for the development of LTi cells.
source: More recently, NFIL3 has been shown also to be required for the development of non-NK ILC1 (Klose et al., 2014), ILC2 (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a), ILC3 (Geiger et al., 2014; Klose et al., 2014; Kobayashi et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a), and LTi cells (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 is essential for the development of all ILC lineages.
source: Thus, NFIL3 is essential for the development of all ILC lineages.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the cited literature and the manuscript's own findings.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice had lowered frequencies and absolute numbers of ILC2, ILC3 (including the NKp46+ subtype), cNK cells, and non-NK ILC1.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed that Nfil3−/− mice had lowered frequencies and absolute numbers of ILC2, ILC3 (including the NKp46+ subtype), cNK cells, and non-NK ILC1 (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice had fewer and smaller Peyer's patches in the small intestine.
source: Nfil3−/− mice also had fewer and smaller Peyer's patches in the small intestine and remaining Peyer's patches contained fewer LTi cells (RORγt+ LTβ+) than wild-type mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating a deficiency in LTi cells that is consistent with the prior reports (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Remaining Peyer's patches in Nfil3−/− mice contained fewer LTi cells (RORγt+ LTβ+) than wild-type mice.
source: Nfil3−/− mice also had fewer and smaller Peyer's patches in the small intestine and remaining Peyer's patches contained fewer LTi cells (RORγt+ LTβ+) than wild-type mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating a deficiency in LTi cells that is consistent with the prior reports (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The requirement for NFIL3 in ILC development is intrinsic to bone marrow progenitors.
source: These data indicate that the requirement for NFIL3 in ILC development is intrinsic to bone marrow progenitors.
evidence: Demonstrated by LSK co-transfer experiments showing reduced ILC generation from Nfil3−/− LSK cells.

claim: Nfil3−/− LSK cells generated fewer ILC2, ILC3, and NK1.1+ ILC3 in the small intestine, and fewer cNK and non-NK ILC1 in the liver.
source: Nfil3−/− LSK cells generated fewer ILC2, ILC3, and NK1.1+ ILC3 in the small intestine, and fewer cNK and non-NK ILC1 in the liver (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by LSK co-transfer experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CLP cells are present in normal numbers in the bone marrow of Nfil3−/− mice.
source: Like LSK cells, CLP cells are also present in normal numbers in the bone marrow of Nfil3−/− mice (Figure 2A) (Male et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014b).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations.

claim: The requirement for NFIL3 in ILC development is intrinsic to the CLP.
source: These findings reveal that the requirement for NFIL3 in ILC development is intrinsic to the CLP and are consistent with the findings of Seillet et al. (Seillet et al., 2014a).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLP co-transfer experiments and supported by citation.

claim: Nfil3−/− CLP had generated fewer ILC2, ILC3 in the small intestine and fewer CD90+ cNK and non-NK ILC1 in the liver.
source: 5 weeks later, Nfil3−/− CLP had generated fewer ILC2, ILC3 in the small intestine and fewer CD90+ cNK and non-NK ILC1 in the liver (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by CLP co-transfer experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Overall T and B cell numbers are not altered in Nfil3−/− mice.
source: In contrast to ILC numbers, overall T and B cell numbers are not altered in Nfil3−/− mice (Kashiwada et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice had markedly fewer Flt3- α4β7+ CLPs (known as αLPs).
source: Nfil3−/− mice had markedly fewer Flt3- α4β7+ CLPs (known as αLPs) (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which have been shown to differentiate into ILC3 and NK cells (Possot et al., 2011).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: αLPs have been shown to differentiate into ILC3 and NK cells.
source: Nfil3−/− mice had markedly fewer Flt3- α4β7+ CLPs (known as αLPs) (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which have been shown to differentiate into ILC3 and NK cells (Possot et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice had fewer ILC2 progenitor cells (ILC2P).
source: Nfil3−/− mice also had fewer previously identified precursor cells that have a more restricted differentiation potential. These cells include ILC2 progenitor cells (ILC2P, Lin− α4β7+ CD127+ Sca1+ CD25+) that only differentiate into ILC2 (Hoyler et al., 2012) (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and the CHILP that can give rise to non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and NK1.1+ NKp46+ ILC3 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ILC2P only differentiate into ILC2.
source: Nfil3−/− mice also had fewer previously identified precursor cells that have a more restricted differentiation potential. These cells include ILC2 progenitor cells (ILC2P, Lin− α4β7+ CD127+ Sca1+ CD25+) that only differentiate into ILC2 (Hoyler et al., 2012) (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and the CHILP that can give rise to non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and NK1.1+ NKp46+ ILC3 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice had fewer CHILP.
source: Nfil3−/− mice also had fewer previously identified precursor cells that have a more restricted differentiation potential. These cells include ILC2 progenitor cells (ILC2P, Lin− α4β7+ CD127+ Sca1+ CD25+) that only differentiate into ILC2 (Hoyler et al., 2012) (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and the CHILP that can give rise to non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and NK1.1+ NKp46+ ILC3 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CHILP can give rise to non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and NK1.1+ NKp46+ ILC3.
source: Nfil3−/− mice also had fewer previously identified precursor cells that have a more restricted differentiation potential. These cells include ILC2 progenitor cells (ILC2P, Lin− α4β7+ CD127+ Sca1+ CD25+) that only differentiate into ILC2 (Hoyler et al., 2012) (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and the CHILP that can give rise to non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and NK1.1+ NKp46+ ILC3 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work.

claim: NFIL3 has been found to be critical for generation of the earliest NK-committed precursors (PreNKP).
source: Similarly, NFIL3 has been found to be critical for generation of the earliest NK-committed precursors (PreNKP) (Male et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice have reduced numbers of precursors that give rise to cNK cells, non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and ILC3.
source: Thus, Nfil3−/− mice have reduced numbers of precursors that give rise to cNK cells, non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and ILC3.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: NFIL3 is required for generation of ILC precursors in the bone marrow.
source: Together, these data indicate that NFIL3 is required for generation of ILC precursors in the bone marrow.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data showing reduced precursor populations in Nfil3−/− mice.

claim: CHILP can differentiate into non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and NK1.1+ NKp46+ ILC3 but not cNK cells.
source: The CHILP, identified through Id2 lineage tracing studies, can differentiate into non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and NK1.1+ NKp46+ ILC3 but not cNK cells (Klose et al., 2014), and the PLZF-dependent ILCP gives rise to all ILCs except cNK cells (Constantinides et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The PLZF-dependent ILCP gives rise to all ILCs except cNK cells.
source: The CHILP, identified through Id2 lineage tracing studies, can differentiate into non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and NK1.1+ NKp46+ ILC3 but not cNK cells (Klose et al., 2014), and the PLZF-dependent ILCP gives rise to all ILCs except cNK cells (Constantinides et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: cNK cell development is not impaired in Zbtb16−/− mice.
source: These findings accord with the partial ILC deficiencies seen in mice lacking Id2 and Zbtb16 (encoding PLZF) (Boos et al., 2007; Savage et al., 2008). In particular, cNK cell development is not impaired in Zbtb16−/− mice, while Id2−/− mice show cNK developmental defects only during NK maturation (Boos et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Id2−/− mice show cNK developmental defects only during NK maturation.
source: These findings accord with the partial ILC deficiencies seen in mice lacking Id2 and Zbtb16 (encoding PLZF) (Boos et al., 2007; Savage et al., 2008). In particular, cNK cell development is not impaired in Zbtb16−/− mice, while Id2−/− mice show cNK developmental defects only during NK maturation (Boos et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ILC2Ps are lineage-specified progenitors of ILC2s with no appreciable potential to differentiate into cNK cells or ILC3.
source: Similarly, ILC2Ps are lineage-specified progenitors of ILC2s with no appreciable potential to differentiate into cNK cells or ILC3 (Hoyler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: αLP cells can differentiate into both cNK cells and ILC3.
source: In contrast to CHILP, ILCP, and ILC2P, αLP cells can differentiate into both cNK cells and ILC3 (Yoshida et al., 2001; Possot et al., 2011) and thus likely represent an earlier stage of ILC development.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: αLPs likely represent an earlier stage of ILC development than CHILP, ILCP, and ILC2P.
source: In contrast to CHILP, ILCP, and ILC2P, αLP cells can differentiate into both cNK cells and ILC3 (Yoshida et al., 2001; Possot et al., 2011) and thus likely represent an earlier stage of ILC development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the broader differentiation potential of αLPs compared to other progenitors.

claim: Similar to CLP and CHILP, αLPs do not express transcription factors that specify ILC lineages, such as RORγt, GATA3, T-BET and EOMES.
source: Similar to CLP and CHILP, αLPs do not express transcription factors that specify ILC lineages, such as RORγt, GATA3, T-BET and EOMES, suggesting an undifferentiated phenotype.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis of transcription factor expression shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only a small fraction of αLPs are ID2+.
source: However, in contrast to CHILPs, which uniformly express high levels of ID2, only a small fraction of αLPs are ID2+ (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The majority of αLPs express ID2 at levels that are markedly lower than those in CHILPs.
source: The majority of αLPs express ID2 at levels that are markedly lower than those in CHILPs.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ID2 is virtually undetectable in CLPs.
source: Because ID2 is virtually undetectable in CLPs, this suggests that αLPs may represent a transitional stage between CLP and CHILP.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: αLPs may represent a transitional stage between CLP and CHILP.
source: Because ID2 is virtually undetectable in CLPs, this suggests that αLPs may represent a transitional stage between CLP and CHILP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the intermediate ID2 expression levels in αLPs.

claim: αLPs do not express PLZF while a major fraction of CHILPs express PLZF.
source: This is further supported by the fact that αLPs do not express PLZF while a major fraction of CHILPs express PLZF (Klose et al., 2014), which defines another group of ILC precursors (ILCP) that lack cNK cell differentiation potential (Constantinides et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: PLZF defines another group of ILC precursors (ILCP) that lack cNK cell differentiation potential.
source: This is further supported by the fact that αLPs do not express PLZF while a major fraction of CHILPs express PLZF (Klose et al., 2014), which defines another group of ILC precursors (ILCP) that lack cNK cell differentiation potential (Constantinides et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: αLPs readily developed into ILC2 when co-cultured with OP9-DL1 cells in the presence of ILC2-inducing cytokines.
source: When co-cultured with OP9-DL1 cells in the presence of ILC2-inducing cytokines, αLPs readily developed into ILC2 as the majority of progeny cells expressed ILC2 markers (GATA3+ Sca1+) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro differentiation assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When OP9-GFP cells (not expressing Notch ligand) were used in the αLP differentiation assay, only a small fraction of progeny cells became ILC2.
source: When OP9-GFP cells (not expressing Notch ligand) were used in this assay, only a small fraction of progeny cells became ILC2 (Figure 3A), confirming that Notch signaling is important for ILC2 differentiation in vitro (Wong et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro differentiation assays shown in Figure 3A and supported by citations.

claim: Notch signaling is important for ILC2 differentiation in vitro.
source: When OP9-GFP cells (not expressing Notch ligand) were used in this assay, only a small fraction of progeny cells became ILC2 (Figure 3A), confirming that Notch signaling is important for ILC2 differentiation in vitro (Wong et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by the current data.

claim: αLP differentiated into ILC3 and RORγt− NK1.1+ cells under ILC3-inducing conditions.
source: In agreement with a prior study (Possot et al., 2011), αLP differentiated into ILC3 and RORγt− NK1.1+ cells under ILC3-inducing conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro differentiation assays shown in Figure 3A and supported by citation.

claim: ILC2 that had differentiated from engrafted αLPs were detected in small intestine and colon of recipient mice after 5 weeks.
source: After 5 weeks, ILC2 that had differentiated from engrafted αLPs were detected in small intestine and colon of the recipient mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transfer experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GATA3+ ILC2 comprised a small fraction of CD127+ ILCs in the small intestine but were the majority in the colon.
source: We noted that GATA3+ ILC2 comprised a small fraction of CD127+ ILCs in the small intestine but were the majority in the colon while RORγt+ ILC3 showed the reverse tissue distribution pattern (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transfer experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RORγt+ ILC3 comprised the majority of CD127+ ILCs in the small intestine but were a small fraction in the colon.
source: We noted that GATA3+ ILC2 comprised a small fraction of CD127+ ILCs in the small intestine but were the majority in the colon while RORγt+ ILC3 showed the reverse tissue distribution pattern (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transfer experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Tissue-specific microenvironment influences ILC development or recruitment.
source: This suggests that tissue-specific microenvironment influences ILC development or recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential tissue distribution of ILC subsets.

claim: Donor αLP cells gave rise to cNK cells in the liver.
source: Consistent with the previously reported cNK cell differentiation potential of αLPs (Possot et al., 2011), donor cells gave rise to cNK cells in the liver, and also differentiated into non-NK ILC1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transfer experiments shown in Figure 3C and supported by citation.

claim: Donor αLP cells differentiated into non-NK ILC1 in the liver.
source: Consistent with the previously reported cNK cell differentiation potential of αLPs (Possot et al., 2011), donor cells gave rise to cNK cells in the liver, and also differentiated into non-NK ILC1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transfer experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No donor-derived B cells were detected in the spleen and small intestine of recipient mice following αLP transfer.
source: Differentiation of ILCs from αLPs was not caused by contamination of αLPs with CLPs, as no donor-derived B cells were detected in the spleen and small intestine of recipient mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transfer experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: αLPs have lost B cell differentiation potential.
source: This accords with the loss of B cell differentiation potential in αLPs (Yoshida et al., 2001; Possot et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by the current data.

claim: There were small numbers of donor-derived T cells in both the small intestine and spleen following αLP transfer.
source: However, there were small numbers of donor-derived T cells, consistent with prior findings that αLP retain some T cell differentiation potential (Possot et al., 2011).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transfer experiments shown in Figure 3D and supported by citation.

claim: αLP retain some T cell differentiation potential.
source: However, there were small numbers of donor-derived T cells, consistent with prior findings that αLP retain some T cell differentiation potential (Possot et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by the current data.

claim: αLPs can give rise to all known ILC lineages in vitro and in vivo.
source: Thus, αLPs can give rise to all known ILC lineages in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the differentiation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: αLPs are likely to be developmentally upstream of CHILP, ILCP, and ILC2P.
source: Given the more restricted differentiation potential of CHILP, ILCP, and ILC2P, αLPs are therefore likely to be developmentally upstream of these progenitors, and defective αLP development in Nfil3−/− mice can thus explain the general ILC deficiency in these mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the broader differentiation potential of αLPs.

claim: Defective αLP development in Nfil3−/− mice can explain the general ILC deficiency in these mice.
source: Given the more restricted differentiation potential of CHILP, ILCP, and ILC2P, αLPs are therefore likely to be developmentally upstream of these progenitors, and defective αLP development in Nfil3−/− mice can thus explain the general ILC deficiency in these mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced αLP numbers and their broad differentiation potential.

claim: When αLP cells acquire CXCR6 expression, they continue to give rise to cNK cells and ILC3 but lose T cell differentiation potential.
source: Prior studies have shown that when αLP cells acquire CXCR6 expression, they continue to give rise to cNK cells and ILC3 but lose T cell differentiation potential (Possot et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CXCR6+ cells comprised 3–4% of the αLP population in the bone marrows of adult wild-type and Nfil3−/− mice.
source: CXCR6+ cells comprised 3–4% of the αLP population in the bone marrows of adult wild-type and Nfil3−/− mice (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absolute numbers of CXCR6+ αLP cells were diminished in Nfil3−/− mice.
source: Their absolute numbers were diminished in Nfil3−/− mice (Figure 4B), in parallel with the decrease in total αLP numbers (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CXCR6+ αLP cells failed to give rise to T cells in any of the clones examined.
source: In contrast to CXCR6- αLP cells, which retained the ability to differentiate into T cells, CXCR6+ αLP cells failed to give rise to T cells in any of the clones examined (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by clonal differentiation assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CXCR6- αLP cells retained the ability to differentiate into T cells.
source: In contrast to CXCR6- αLP cells, which retained the ability to differentiate into T cells, CXCR6+ αLP cells failed to give rise to T cells in any of the clones examined (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by clonal differentiation assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mixtures of cNK, non-NK ILC1, ILC2, and ILC3 cells were present in the progeny populations of single CXCR6+ αLP cells.
source: While no T cells were detected, mixtures of cNK, non-NK ILC1, ILC2, and ILC3 cells were present in the progeny populations of single CXCR6+ αLP cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by clonal differentiation assays shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Approximately 60% of wells with clonal growth from CXCR6+ αLP cells contained multiple ILC lineages.
source: Approximately 60% of wells with clonal growth contained multiple ILC lineages.
evidence: Demonstrated by clonal differentiation assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 43.3% of the wells differentiated from individual CXCR6+ αLP cells contained two ILC lineages.
source: In particular, 43.3% of the wells differentiated from individual CXCR6+ αLP cells contained two ILC lineages, and 11.7% three ILC lineages (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by clonal differentiation assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 11.7% of wells differentiated from individual CXCR6+ αLP cells contained three ILC lineages.
source: In particular, 43.3% of the wells differentiated from individual CXCR6+ αLP cells contained two ILC lineages, and 11.7% three ILC lineages (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by clonal differentiation assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 2.5% of wells differentiated from individual CXCR6+ αLP cells contained all four ILC lineages.
source: Importantly, 2.5% of wells contained all four ILC lineages, demonstrating that individual CXCR6+ αLP cells can differentiate into all known ILC lineages.
evidence: Demonstrated by clonal differentiation assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Individual CXCR6+ αLP cells can differentiate into all known ILC lineages.
source: Importantly, 2.5% of wells contained all four ILC lineages, demonstrating that individual CXCR6+ αLP cells can differentiate into all known ILC lineages.
evidence: Demonstrated by clonal differentiation assays showing wells with all four ILC lineages.

claim: CXCR6+ αLP cells differentiated into cNK, non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and ILC3, but not B cells or T cells, when transferred into sublethally-irradiated Rag2−/−;Il2rg−/− mice.
source: In agreement with the in vitro differentiation data, CXCR6+ αLP cells differentiated into cNK, non-NK ILC1, ILC2 and ILC3, but not B cells or T cells, when transferred into sublethally-irradiated Rag2−/−;Il2rg−/− mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo transfer experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CXCR6+ αLP cells include committed ILC precursors that can differentiate into all major ILC lineages in vitro and in vivo.
source: Thus, CXCR6+ αLP cells include committed ILC precursors that can differentiate into all major ILC lineages in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the clonal differentiation and in vivo transfer data.

claim: Nfil3 expression was readily detected in CLPs.
source: Nfil3 expression was readily detected in CLPs (Figure 5A), which accords with previous reports (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014b) and is consistent with the finding that NFIL3 regulates ILC development in a CLP-intrinsic manner (Figure 1C; Seillet et al., 2014a).
evidence: Demonstrated by microarray data shown in Figure 5A and supported by citations.

claim: There was no detectable expression in CLPs of other transcription factors that are known to govern ILC development, including Id2, Zbtb16, Eomes, Tcf7, Rora, Rorc, Gata3 and Tbx21.
source: However, there was no detectable expression in CLPs of other transcription factors that are known to govern ILC development (Figure 5A). These factors include Id2 (Hoyler et al., 2012; Male et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014b), Zbtb16 (Constantinides et al., 2014), Eomes (Male et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014b), Tcf7 (encoding TCF-1) (Yang et al., 2013), Rora (Wong et al., 2012), Rorc (Eberl and Littman, 2003; Sawa et al., 2010), Gata3 (Hoyler et al., 2012) and Tbx21 (Gordon et al., 2012; Rankin et al., 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by microarray data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tox was expressed at a detectable level in wild-type CLPs and was down-regulated in Nfil3−/− CLPs.
source: In contrast, the high mobility group (HMG) transcriptional regulator Tox, which is known to regulate NK and ILC3 development (Aliahmad et al., 2010), was expressed at a detectable level in wild-type CLPs and was down-regulated in Nfil3−/− CLPs (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by microarray and Q-PCR data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: TOX is known to regulate NK and ILC3 development.
source: In contrast, the high mobility group (HMG) transcriptional regulator Tox, which is known to regulate NK and ILC3 development (Aliahmad et al., 2010), was expressed at a detectable level in wild-type CLPs and was down-regulated in Nfil3−/− CLPs (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 regulates Tox expression in EL4 cells.
source: As an alternative, we found that NFIL3 regulates Tox expression in EL4 cells, a mouse lymphoma cell line (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by knockdown and overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of NFIL3 in EL4 cells with two independent shRNA constructs led to dose-dependent down-regulation of Tox expression.
source: Knockdown of NFIL3 in EL4 cells with two independent shRNA constructs led to dose-dependent down-regulation of Tox expression (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of NFIL3 in EL4 cells increased Tox expression.
source: Conversely, overexpression of NFIL3 in EL4 cells increased Tox expression (Figure 5C), indicating that Tox expression is sensitive to NFIL3 levels in EL4 cells in a manner similar to CLPs.
evidence: Demonstrated by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Tox expression is sensitive to NFIL3 levels in EL4 cells in a manner similar to CLPs.
source: Conversely, overexpression of NFIL3 in EL4 cells increased Tox expression (Figure 5C), indicating that Tox expression is sensitive to NFIL3 levels in EL4 cells in a manner similar to CLPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar regulatory relationship observed in both cell types.

claim: NFIL3 directly bound to the Tox promoter (nt −2105 to −1867).
source: A chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay with an NFIL3-specific antibody (Yu et al., 2013) demonstrated that NFIL3 directly bound to the Tox promoter (nt −2105 to −1867) and that overexpression of NFIL3 enhanced this binding (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP assays shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Overexpression of NFIL3 enhanced binding to the Tox promoter.
source: A chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay with an NFIL3-specific antibody (Yu et al., 2013) demonstrated that NFIL3 directly bound to the Tox promoter (nt −2105 to −1867) and that overexpression of NFIL3 enhanced this binding (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP assays shown in Figure 5D.

claim: NFIL3 activated Tox promoter activity as assessed by a luciferase reporter assay.
source: Finally, NFIL3 activated Tox promoter activity as assessed by a luciferase reporter assay (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 5E.

claim: NFIL3 activates Tox expression by directly binding to its promoter.
source: Thus, NFIL3 activates Tox expression by directly binding to its promoter.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the ChIP and luciferase reporter data.

claim: Tox is essential for cNK and ILC3 development.
source: Because Tox is known to be essential for cNK and ILC3 development (Aliahmad et al., 2010), we postulated that lowered Tox expression leads to the broad ILC deficiency in Nfil3−/− mice and that restoring Tox expression would rescue ILC development.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Transduction of a TOX-encoding plasmid into Nfil3−/− LSK cells led to increased numbers of cNK cells in spleen, non-NK ILC1 cells in liver, and ILC2 and ILC3 in the small intestines of recipient mice.
source: Compared to the empty vector control, transduction of the TOX-encoding plasmid led to increased numbers of cNK cells in spleen, non-NK ILC1 cells in liver, and ILC2 and ILC3 in the small intestines of recipient mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Rescue of ILC development from Nfil3−/− LSK cells by Tox was largely comparable to rescue by Nfil3.
source: We observed that rescue of ILC development from Nfil3−/− LSK cells by Tox was largely comparable to rescue by Nfil3 in the same setting, supporting the idea that Tox acts downstream of Nfil3 in ILC development.
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ILC development is rescued by restoring Tox expression in Nfil3−/− progenitors.
source: Thus, ILC development is rescued by restoring Tox expression in Nfil3−/− progenitors, indicating that NFIL3 drives ILC development in part by regulating Tox expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: NFIL3 drives ILC development in part by regulating Tox expression.
source: Thus, ILC development is rescued by restoring Tox expression in Nfil3−/− progenitors, indicating that NFIL3 drives ILC development in part by regulating Tox expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: IL-22 is produced both by ILC3 and TH17 cells.
source: IL-22 is produced both by ILC3 and TH17 cells and is essential for protection against Citrobacter rodentium infection (Satoh-Takayama et al., 2008; Zheng et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IL-22 is essential for protection against Citrobacter rodentium infection.
source: IL-22 is produced both by ILC3 and TH17 cells and is essential for protection against Citrobacter rodentium infection (Satoh-Takayama et al., 2008; Zheng et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice show elevated susceptibility to intestinal pathogens such as Citrobacter rodentium.
source: Nfil3−/− mice show elevated susceptibility to intestinal pathogens such as Citrobacter rodentium (Geiger et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice retain TH17 cells, which are elevated relative to wild-type mice.
source: However, Nfil3−/− mice retain TH17 cells, which are elevated relative to wild-type mice (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nfil3−/−;Rag1−/− mice were more susceptible to oral C. rodentium infection than Rag1−/− mice as measured by weight loss.
source: Nfil3−/−;Rag1−/− mice were more susceptible to oral C. rodentium infection than Rag1−/− mice as measured by weight loss (Figure 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: NFIL3-dependent ILC development is essential for host immune defense against a mucosal pathogen.
source: These data thus suggest that NFIL3-dependent ILC development is essential for host immune defense against a mucosal pathogen.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased susceptibility of Nfil3−/−;Rag1−/− mice to C. rodentium infection.

claim: NFIL3 directs the development of bone marrow precursors, derived from the CLP, which give rise to all known ILC lineages including cNK cells.
source: Here we present new insight into the fundamental role of the basic leucine zipper transcription factor NFIL3 in ILC development. We show that NFIL3 directs the development of bone marrow precursors, derived from the CLP, which give rise to all known ILC lineages including cNK cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: NFIL3 regulates the expression of the transcription factor TOX.
source: Additionally, we show that NFIL3 regulates the expression of the transcription factor TOX, and provide evidence that a NFIL3-TOX transcription factor cascade is central to the development of all ILC lineages.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: A NFIL3-TOX transcription factor cascade is central to the development of all ILC lineages.
source: Additionally, we show that NFIL3 regulates the expression of the transcription factor TOX, and provide evidence that a NFIL3-TOX transcription factor cascade is central to the development of all ILC lineages.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the regulatory relationship and rescue experiments.

claim: All ILC subsets express Id2.
source: Several transcription factors are known to play essential roles in ILC development. For example, all ILC subsets express Id2, an antagonist of E proteins that control B- and T- cell commitment (Kee, 2009; Hoyler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Id2 is an antagonist of E proteins that control B- and T- cell commitment.
source: Several transcription factors are known to play essential roles in ILC development. For example, all ILC subsets express Id2, an antagonist of E proteins that control B- and T- cell commitment (Kee, 2009; Hoyler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of Id2 in mice abrogates the development of multiple ILC lineages.
source: Deletion of Id2 in mice abrogates the development of multiple ILC lineages (Yokota et al., 1999; Hoyler et al., 2012), although NK developmental defects arise only during NK maturation (Boos et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TOX is required for the development of cNK cells and ILC3.
source: The HMG factor TOX is required for the development of cNK cells and ILC3 (Aliahmad et al., 2010), and the transcription factor PLZF is required for the differentiation of non-NK cell ILC subsets (Constantinides et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The transcription factor PLZF is required for the differentiation of non-NK cell ILC subsets.
source: The HMG factor TOX is required for the development of cNK cells and ILC3 (Aliahmad et al., 2010), and the transcription factor PLZF is required for the differentiation of non-NK cell ILC subsets (Constantinides et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 was found to be essential for the development of all known ILC lineages, including cNK cells.
source: Most recently, the basic leucine zipper transcription factor NFIL3 was found to be essential for the development of all known ILC lineages, including cNK cells (Geiger et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 activation of TOX expression is a key mechanism by which NFIL3 directs ILC development.
source: Our findings suggest that NFIL3 activation of TOX expression is a key mechanism by which NFIL3 directs ILC development.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the regulatory relationship and rescue experiments.

claim: Forced Tox expression in Nfil3−/− bone marrow progenitors rescues the ILC developmental defect and restores differentiation of cNK, non-NK ILC1, ILC2, and ILC3.
source: This idea is supported by our finding that forced Tox expression in Nfil3−/− bone marrow progenitors rescues the ILC developmental defect and restores differentiation of cNK, non-NK ILC1, ILC2, and ILC3.
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: A NFIL3-TOX transcription factor cascade plays a fundamental role in the development of all ILC lineages.
source: Together, these data support the idea that a NFIL3-TOX transcription factor cascade plays a fundamental role in the development of all ILC lineages.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the regulatory relationship and rescue experiments.

claim: Forced expression of Eomes can rescue cNK cell development from Nfil3−/− hematopoietic progenitors.
source: Recent studies have shown that forced expression of Eomes can rescue cNK cell development from Nfil3−/− hematopoietic progenitors (Male et al., 2014; Seillet et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Eomes is not expressed in CLPs.
source: However, because Eomes is not expressed in CLPs (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and Eomes deficiency only impacts cNK cells but no other ILCs (Klose et al., 2014), Eomes is unlikely to mediate the NFIL3-dependent development of non-NK ILCs, and may lie developmentally downstream of NFIL3-TOX during NK cell development.
evidence: Demonstrated by microarray data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Eomes deficiency only impacts cNK cells but no other ILCs.
source: However, because Eomes is not expressed in CLPs (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and Eomes deficiency only impacts cNK cells but no other ILCs (Klose et al., 2014), Eomes is unlikely to mediate the NFIL3-dependent development of non-NK ILCs, and may lie developmentally downstream of NFIL3-TOX during NK cell development.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Eomes is unlikely to mediate the NFIL3-dependent development of non-NK ILCs.
source: However, because Eomes is not expressed in CLPs (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and Eomes deficiency only impacts cNK cells but no other ILCs (Klose et al., 2014), Eomes is unlikely to mediate the NFIL3-dependent development of non-NK ILCs, and may lie developmentally downstream of NFIL3-TOX during NK cell development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of Eomes expression in CLPs and its specific role in cNK cells.

claim: Eomes may lie developmentally downstream of NFIL3-TOX during NK cell development.
source: However, because Eomes is not expressed in CLPs (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and Eomes deficiency only impacts cNK cells but no other ILCs (Klose et al., 2014), Eomes is unlikely to mediate the NFIL3-dependent development of non-NK ILCs, and may lie developmentally downstream of NFIL3-TOX during NK cell development.
evidence: This is speculation based on the regulatory relationships and expression patterns.

claim: Certain NK cells, including salivary gland NK cells, are not impacted by Nfil3 deficiency.
source: Although NFIL3 is required for the development of the major ILC types and their precursors, some ILC subtypes appear to be NFIL3-independent. For example, certain NK cells, including salivary gland NK cells (Cortez et al., 2014) and tissue-resident NK cells (Sojka et al., 2014), are not impacted by Nfil3 deficiency, in contrast to conventional NK cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Tissue-resident NK cells are not impacted by Nfil3 deficiency.
source: Although NFIL3 is required for the development of the major ILC types and their precursors, some ILC subtypes appear to be NFIL3-independent. For example, certain NK cells, including salivary gland NK cells (Cortez et al., 2014) and tissue-resident NK cells (Sojka et al., 2014), are not impacted by Nfil3 deficiency, in contrast to conventional NK cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Extramedullary development of thymic NK cells is independent of NFIL3.
source: Extramedullary development of thymic NK cells is also independent of NFIL3 (Crotta et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: During mouse cytomegalovirus infection, NK cells in Nfil3−/− mice expand to numbers similar to those in wild-type mice through an IL-15-dependent mechanism.
source: In addition, during mouse cytomegalovirus infection, NK cells in Nfil3−/− mice expand to numbers similar to those in wild-type mice through an IL-15-dependent mechanism (Firth et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The requirement for NFIL3 can be overridden by cytokine signaling during infection.
source: This suggests that the requirement for NFIL3 can be overridden by cytokine signaling during infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IL-15-dependent NK cell expansion during infection.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice appear to have normal lymph nodes.
source: Finally, despite the strict requirement for NFIL3 in bone marrow ILC precursor development (αLP and CHILP), Nfil3−/− mice appear to have normal lymph nodes (Spits and Di Santo, 2011; Seillet et al., 2014b) and only moderately impaired Peyer's patch development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)(Geiger et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nfil3−/− mice have only moderately impaired Peyer's patch development.
source: Finally, despite the strict requirement for NFIL3 in bone marrow ILC precursor development (αLP and CHILP), Nfil3−/− mice appear to have normal lymph nodes (Spits and Di Santo, 2011; Seillet et al., 2014b) and only moderately impaired Peyer's patch development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)(Geiger et al., 2014).
evidence: Demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation.

claim: Fetal LTi cell function may be preserved in the absence of Nfil3.
source: One possibility is that fetal LTi cell function may be preserved in the absence of Nfil3, which could account for the presence of lymph nodes in Nfil3−/− mice.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the presence of lymph nodes in Nfil3−/− mice.

claim: Nfil3 is regulated by the circadian clock and its expression varies diurnally in multiple tissues and cells.
source: Nfil3 is regulated by the circadian clock and thus its expression varies diurnally in multiple tissues and cells (Duez et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nfil3 expression varies diurnally in T cells.
source: We previously showed that Nfil3 expression varies diurnally in T cells and that NFIL3 synchronizes TH17 lineage specification to the day-night light cycle (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NFIL3 synchronizes TH17 lineage specification to the day-night light cycle.
source: We previously showed that Nfil3 expression varies diurnally in T cells and that NFIL3 synchronizes TH17 lineage specification to the day-night light cycle (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Circadian disruption by chronic light cycle perturbation elevates intestinal TH17 cell frequencies and increases susceptibility to intestinal inflammation.
source: Synchronization is essential for TH17 cell homeostasis, as circadian disruption by chronic light cycle perturbation elevates intestinal TH17 cell frequencies and increases susceptibility to intestinal inflammation (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Precursor differentiation may be synchronized with diurnal light cycles through a similar mechanism to TH17 cells.
source: The finding that NFIL3 is required for the development of committed ILC precursors suggests that precursor differentiation may also be synchronized with diurnal light cycles through a similar mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known role of NFIL3 in circadian regulation of TH17 cells.

claim: Identification of a committed pan-ILC precursor should allow further insight into the developmental pathways that drive ILC cell fate decisions.
source: Altogether, our findings provide new insight into the defining role of NFIL3 in ILC development. Identification of a committed pan-ILC precursor should allow further insight into the developmental pathways that drive ILC cell fate decisions.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: NFIL3-dependent pathways may provide new targets for treatment of inflammatory and infectious diseases.
source: Because of the general importance of ILCs in immune defense, NFIL3-dependent pathways may provide new targets for treatment of inflammatory and infectious diseases.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications.
